Read our privacy notice. Count Binface has taken digs at Nigel Farage in his manifesto for the Clacton by-election. The “space and electoral warrior” beamed out his 20-point platform for the contest triggered by the Reform UK leader quitting as MP for the Essex seaside constituency as he faced a swirl of financial allegations. * MPs who resign mid-Parliament to be banned from the resulting by-election * I promise to spend more time in Clacton-on-Sea than in Washington DC, and to champion the area * I will not accept £5 million gifts from crypto billionaires (on Earth) Mr Farage will face a record 33 rival candidates in the by-election on August 13. The main Westminster parties are boycotting the contest, dismissing it as a stunt by the Reform UK leader. He wanted the by-election to be a “people versus the establishment” showdown. But his move is threatening to backfire as the contest could turn into a largely two-way battle between him and Count Binface, the character created by comedian Jon Harvey, despite the huge number of other contenders. Other pledges by the Count include that 99 Flake ice-creams to cost no more than 99p, arcade grabber games to be made fairer so players “actually have a change to win”, Parliament to be moved “to my new  Bin HQ” while the Palace of Westminster is restored, and Wayne Rooney to be “new expert summariser for BBC” at Eurovision. The Binface v Farage battle has already gone global, being reported in America, Australia, India, France, Italy and many other countries around the world. On a more serious note, Reform UK is facing a growing number of allegations over its financial affairs. A probe by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards into Mr Farage, over a £5 million gift from Reform donor Christopher Harborne before becoming an MP, is understood to have been paused after he quit Parliament. The Reform leader is also facing calls for an investigation following reports that long-term ally George Cottrell had provided undeclared funding for security and staffing in the year before he was elected. Mr Cottrell reportedly recruited and paid three staff to work on Mr Farage’s social media before the general election, and had continued to allow him to use a five-storey Georgian property he rented near Buckingham Palace. Mr Farage denies any wrongdoing and says he followed Commons rules. The Reform leader, an ally of Donald Trump, has also rejected claims that he spends little time in Clacton. If Mr Farage is found to have breached Commons rules on declaring interests and is suspended for more than 10 sitting days, it could trigger a recall petition, potentially leading to a second Clacton by-election. New PM pledges 'circuit breaker' Tendring District Council said a total of 34 candidates had entered the August 13 race, which is believed to be a record for a parliamentary contest. The council said the previous record is understood to have been 26 candidates, set at the Haltemprice and Howden by-election in July 2008, which was triggered by Tory Sir David Davis in his own seat and similarly ignored by the main Westminster parties. Separately, Reform Deputy Leader Richard Tice is facing allegations over funding for the party.                     Graham Dunbar, Associated Press GENEVA (AP) — One week after the World Cup final, FIFA President Gianni Infantino attacked perceived critics for "spreading hate and false rumors" about the tournament. Infantino praised FIFA for "delivering the best show in the world" and spoke of the World Cup bringing "joy and togetherness," in a 900-word statement published across a 15-page post on his Instagram account and on FIFA's website late Sunday. "Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," the FIFA leader wrote, addressing his comments to "those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumors." READ MORE: FIFA's Infantino targeted by complaint to Olympic ethics body after Trump lobbying on Balogun ban FIFA and Infantino faced criticism during the World Cup for Iran team officials, a Somali referee and fans being denied entry to the United States; alleged political influence by U.S. President Donald Trump in letting Folarin Balogun avoid a ban for a red card; unprecedented high ticket prices and commercialized breaks in play midway through each half of all 104 games. "Every city was packed with fans from all around the globe," Infantino wrote. "While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate." "While you hide, we are exploring the streets of Canada, Mexico, and the United States, talking with fans, engaging with people, and ensuring everyone's safety." Infantino has an increasingly testy relationship with media during the 11th year of his presidency. His eve-of-tournament news conference in Mexico City was his first with a full gathering of international media since March 2023. The previous such news conference in Rwanda, after his reelection by acclaim from FIFA member federations, saw Infantino ask his audience: "Why are you so mean?" READ MORE: FIFA's Infantino defends World Cup ticket prices, says fans 'should chill' about ref denied US entry In Mexico City last month, Infantino suggested critics should "chill, relax." And he's coming under scrutiny from some in the U.S. Congress. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, sent Infantino a letter on Sunday seeking documents detailing ties between FIFA and the Trump administration. A representative for FIFA didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter. Iran's ability to play at least three games in the U.S. was a key pretournament issue, and the squad made a late switch to a training camp in Tijuana, Mexico instead of Tucson, Arizona. "Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict," Infantino noted in his statement. "While you spread hatred, we worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war." Fans denied visas to enter the U.S. included Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, the celebrated statue supporter of Congo which was dealing with an Ebola virus outbreak. He attended one game in Mexico. "You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world," Infantino wrote. "Countries facing serious health issues or other challenges were granted visas." On fallout from the red card for U.S. forward Balogun, Infantino claimed "subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine." WATCH: Trump praises 'really brilliant decision' on Balogun's red card after he called FIFA's Infantino FIFA did not overturn Balogun's red card, which does occur in domestic club competitions, but instead took the more unusual step of deferring the one-game ban for a probationary period. FIFA has yet to publish the written verdict of its disciplinary judge. "To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray, or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions," Infantino wrote. Chaos has just released V-Ray 7, update 4, adding final-frame, real-time rendering directly inside supported digital content creation viewports and deeper virtual production integration for media and entertainment pipelines. The update is designed to reduce asset conversions and tool switching by allowing artists to work with the same V-Ray scene from early look development and real-time exploration through virtual production and final rendering, with path-traced feedback available directly inside supported DCC applications. Used across visual effects, animation, product visualization and advertising, V-Ray provides physically accurate lighting and rendering tools for developing shots and producing final images, while connecting more of that work inside the artist’s existing application so scenes and assets can move through production with fewer conversions and less rebuilding. “Artists lose time when a scene has to be converted or rebuilt when it moves between tools,” Allan Poore, Chief Product Officer at Chaos, said. “V-Ray 7, update 4, keeps the same asset moving from early exploration to on-set production and final rendering. That means faster feedback, fewer technical interruptions, and more time to focus on the shot.” Artists can now use Chaos Vantage to explore and assemble V-Ray scenes in real time inside supported DCC viewports without exporting assets to a separate game engine. The workflow is available through a Vantage Hydra Delegate for Houdini and an enhanced Maya Live Link, with 3ds Max integration introduced earlier this year. Support for Blender is coming soon through Live Link, and Chaos is developing an OpenUSD Hydra Delegate to bring Vantage’s real-time rendering and V-Ray’s offline rendering into other host applications, including Nuke and Katana. The release also introduces Gaussian Splat relighting, allowing artists to adjust the lighting of scanned environments in Houdini, Maya, 3ds Max and Vantage. Scanned environments typically capture lighting as part of the original image, making them difficult to match to a 3D scene; the new relighting workflow lets artists use captured environments from previz through final delivery without recreating the location or relying on complex workarounds. “Gaussian Splats have opened up incredible creative possibilities, but lighting has always been the hard part,” Vlado Koylazov, Co-Founder and Head of Innovation at Chaos, said. “Now artists can bring a real, scanned environment into their scene and light it exactly the way the shot needs, instead of being stuck with what the scan gave them.” For virtual production, the same V-Ray scene can move into Chaos Arena for LED wall shoots, giving crews more control over materials, focus and colour while cameras are rolling. Performance updates include GPU interactive previews that can begin up to twice as fast and CPU rendering that is up to 13 percent faster on supported configurations. Light Cache Denoising produces cleaner interactive previews faster, out-of-frustum displacement reduces memory use for geometry of complex surfaces outside the camera view, and Distributed Rendering 2 removes previous machine-count limits for larger jobs. V-Ray 7, update 4 also introduces new artist-friendly tools and workflows designed to reduce the time it takes to reach the desired look and final frame, including: V-Ray 7, update 4 is available now. Full pricing information is available through the Chaos pricing page. The free V-Ray for Blender Community Edition remains available for Windows and macOS through the product page, with a Linux build now also available for download. title: West Indies v Pakistan: Justin Greaves takes five wickets for none in incredible spell - BBC
content: Justin Greaves' figures of 5-27 eclipsed his previous best of 3-39 against Sri Lanka earlier this year West Indies 311 (Hope 92; Ali 4-50) & 126-7 (Chanderpaul 35, Abbas 3-14) West Indies all-rounder Justin Greaves took five wickets without conceding a run in an incredible spell of bowling on day three of the first Test against Pakistan. Greaves, who is playing in his 17th Test, claimed his maiden Test five-wicket haul to help dismiss Pakistan for 282 in response to West Indies' first-innings total of 311. The 32-year-old Barbadian's spell - five consecutive wicket maidens - was all the more remarkable given he had bowled six overs earlier in the day for 27 runs without taking a wicket. "When I came on captain Roston Chase just said 'continue to be disciplined in what you are doing' and to see if I can get some wickets for the team," Greaves said. "The ball nipped around and I got some reward. Anytime I get the ball in hand the team looks to me to be that solid player for them [and] try to dig us out of situations. "To get five wickets for the first time in Test cricket, I'm really happy, but there's still a lot of work to do in the game." Pakistan captain Shan Masood was Greaves' first wicket at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Trinidad when he was bowled for 109 in the 64th over following a superb set-up. Greaves had pushed the ball wide to the left-hander from over the wicket before he tailed a delivery back into Masood who played down the wrong line and inside edged on to his stumps. Aamer Jamal had his middle stump uprooted in Greaves' next over as the seamer speared one through his defences. Greaves then trapped Ali Usman lbw before he had Mohammed Rizwan and Mohammad Abbas both caught behind as Pakistan lost their last seven wickets for just 38 runs. West Indies reached stumps on day three on 126-7 in their second innings - a lead of 155 runs - to leave the match finely poised. title: Mary V. Farrington, 95 - Port City Daily
content: LELAND — It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved mother, Mary V. Farrington. She was able to finish her life in her own home, with her eldest child constantly at her side. She had succumbed to breast cancer which she had been battling for many years. Mom had her wits about her until the end. We were able to celebrate her 95th birthday just a week before she passed. She had a wonderful time and enjoyed a birthday cupcake. Just a few days after, she rapidly went into decline. We believe she stubbornly held on until this birthday party so that she could have all three of her children present as well as her wonderful bridge friends, her grandson Scott and some of her special neighbors. Although Mom always had challenges with her health, she lead a very full and productive life. She was an amazing seamstress who sewed beautiful dresses for her two young daughters. In addition she always volunteered to sew all the recital costumes for all the children in our dance class. She was an avid bridge player and lover of reading. And like many women of her generation, she loved watching the soap operas. She was deeply involved in her church, sang in the choir, lead bible studies, became a deacon, and lead prayer chains for those in need. Mom was smart. She was a straight A student and a member of the national honor society. She was a perfect candidate for college, but the difficult post depression years made that impossible. Mom is now at peace with her husband of 61 years, Stanley C. Farrington. She will be remembered always with love and gratitude by her three children, Sheri German and spouse Andy, Jill Carney and spouse Rob, and George Farrington and spouse Andrea, her five grandchildren, Michael Kossin, David Kossin, Jennifer German Dulany, Scott German, and Courtney Hammons, and by many dear friends. ”What we have once enjoyed we can never lose. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us.” Helen Keller A Celebration of Life will be held at the Zion United Methodist Church located at 6864 Zion Church Rd NE, Leland, NC 28451. We will gather in the coming months when the weather is cooler. The family suggests donations in her memory to Zion United Methodist Church’s Outreach Ministries. content: All eyes will be on America First Field this Wednesday, July 29 as Utah Royals FC welcome star forward Trinity Rodman and the Washington Spirit to the Wasatch Front. The midweek matchup will mark the Royals second of three matches played in a congested nine day period. Following the exciting 4-1 victory over the weekend, the home side will look to continue its dominance in front of the home crowd. This edition of storylines will dive into how the Royals have continued to break records in its strongest season in club history, the squad's impressive ability to work as a unit and URFC’s history with the dominant Washington side. Since dropping two matches in its return to NWSL play following the 2026 FIFA World Cup, URFC has bounced-back, winning two consecutive matches to regain the strong form showcased during the first half of the season. While the Royals may not have what is considered as one “big-name” player like opposing squads, the home side has pointed out the importance of every single player on its roster who have worked tirelessly and as one to boost the Royals in its record breaking season towards the top of the NWSL standings. While the Royals have key attacking pieces on its roster like, Canadian forward Cloé Lacasse and Japanese star Mina Tanaka the squad boasts an impressive nine different goal scorers thus far in 2026, making URFC a difficult team to plan against as any one player from any position can break through to find the back of the net. Utah’s road match against the North Carolina Courage last Saturday, July 25th was the perfect example of this, with four set-piece goals (including penalties) scored by four different players across three different positions. Captain Kate Del Fava opened up the scoring with fellow defender Tatumn Milazzo netting the game winning goal just 18 minutes later, bringing both center backs onto the score sheet in the same match for the first time. While Del Fava earned her first goal in over two years, Milazzo now has a career high three goals in a season. Along with the defenders showcasing brilliance on both ends of the pitch was Tanaka who netted her fifth goal of the season, bringing the Japanese international to an impressive ninth goal contribution of the season (5 goals, 4 assists) to tie Amy Rodriguez (2019) for third in club history. The midfielder continues to bring creativity and high-quality scoring abilities to the pitch, making her a threat to any opposition's defense. The Utah Royals offensive power can not be explained without the impact of Lacasse who’s stoppage time penalty against the Courage helped to lift the Royals to its 4-1 victory and brought the forward to sole ownership of URFC’s 2026 Golden Boot race with six goals and four assists. The veteran brings a speed and fierce presence to the pitch that not only lifts herself but the whole team in earning results. Lacasses’ 10 goal contributions this season have now brought her equal with the Utah Royals single-season club record set by Christen Press in 2019, with 14 matches left in 2026, the Canadian has ample time to write herself further into Utah’s history books. While the Royals attack has been explosive this season, the work of its backline led by goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn has been key in keeping the squad in matches. With five massive saves on Saturday, McGlynn has continued to showcase her high level ability to read the game and remains a force between the posts with 24 saves and four clean sheets on the season. The veteran keeper will need to continue to work seamlessly with her backline in order to earn a result against the explosive attack of Washington on Wednesday. As the Royals gear up to take on league-leading Washington Spirit on Wednesday night it is imperative to look back at the squad's history with the visiting side since its return to Utah in 2024. While the Royals overall record of 1-2-2 (W-L-T) against the Spirit looks to favor the visitors, URFC has remained unbeaten in three straight meetings with Washington, taking one victory and two draws. Most recently, the Royals traveled to Audi Field on March 25, 2026 earning a 1-1 draw. While URFC fell behind in the 18th minute, the visitors refused to quit, continuing to pressure on and off the ball in search of a goal. With a belief that never wavered, Tanaka, fresh off an AFC Asian Cup win, netted the equalizer in the 84th minute to help the squad earn a point in what many consider to be one of the most difficult road environments in the NWSL; Washington's home stadium. The Spirit have continued to be a force in the league, with many goal scoring threats on its roster like Italian forward Sofia Cantore who has four goals and one assist on the season. One main attacking threat the Royals will face on Wednesday is USWNT standout Trinity Rodman. The 24-year-old forward is a force in the offensive third, having used her speed and impressive footwork to net seven goals and five assists thus far in 2026. URFC’s backline will need to work cohesively to thwart any attacks by Rodman in order to keep her off the scoresheet. While the visitors have the attacking power of Rodman, URFC has proven itself as a squad that can exploit opposing defenses and go toe-to-toe with any squad in the NWSL. The key for the Royals in a game where it will undoubtedly see immense pressure, is to get on the scoresheet first. While the home side boasts an impressive 9-2-0 (W-T-L) record when doing so, Washington has yet to lose a match when scoring first earning a 10-0-1 record. Drawing first blood will be an important momentum boost for the home side in its hopes for a victory on Wednesday. The midweek home matchup against the first-place Washington Spirit is scheduled to kickoff at 7 PM MT with tickets still available for purchase. Following Wednesday’s match, URFC remain at America First Field for a second consecutive match, welcoming Sophia Wilson and the Portland Thorns on Sunday, August 2nd. Kickoff is scheduled for 5 PM MT with tickets for both matches are available for purchase here. URFC takes on Washington Spirit at home. title: Socialists v. the Senate - thealpenanews.com
content: Political parties tend to harshly reject the idea that they are a threat to the constitutional order, but the Democratic Socialists of America are making it part of their brand. The DSA has released a new program that, besides contemplating the advent of a classless society, calls for abolishing the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court. This is literally a revolutionary program to topple the American system as we have known it since 1789. It’s the kind of thing you might expect after angry rebels mount the barricades in Washington, D.C., and overthrow the government. It makes proposals to abolish the filibuster seem trifling in comparison and even makes court-packing look relatively moderate. The proposal to kill off the world’s greatest deliberative body has gotten the most attention. New York City’s DSA co-chair, Gustavo Gordillo, went on Fox News to explain that the senate is “undemocratic,” while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said that she opposes the filibuster and elements of the Senate that “were founded on Jim Crow.” Contrary to Gordillo, the Senate is a democratic institution; no one wins a Senate seat without getting more votes than his or her opponent. Yet, part of its role in our system is to serve as a check on popular passions. At the institution’s inception, state legislatures appointed senators. Those days are long gone — the 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, requires direct election — but six-year terms and staggered elections give the Senate more insulation from the transient currents of public sentiment than the House of Representatives. Then there are the senate rules that put an emphasis on consensus and delay. AOC sounded confused when she cited Senate practices created under Jim Crow, the system of formalized racial discrimination that arose about 100 years after the creation of the Senate. It’s true that the filibuster was used as a tool to attempt to block landmark civil rights legislation, without ultimate success. But the filibuster is an instrument of every minority party in the Senate trying to block the agenda of a president of the opposing party, very much including Senate Democrats arrayed against President Trump today. The Senate has another function, which is giving small states equal representation with large states. This is the source of the charge that it is undemocratic. Why should Wyoming, population roughly 600,000, have as many senators as California, population nearly 40 million? This is meant, though, to keep large states from having overwhelming influence on the nation’s governance, and to give easy-to-ignore places a say in the nation’s affairs. For proportional representation, there’s the House; California has 52 members of Congress, whereas Wyoming has one. All this said, regardless of the merits, the Constitution deems the provision of equal senators for the states un-amendable: “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” This suggests that the dissolution of the constitutional system couldn’t be achieved by constitutional means, since the Founders didn’t supply a readily available self-destruct button for their brilliant handiwork. Not that the DSA cares. What they are seeking would, in some ways, be a return to the Articles of Confederation, under which we had a unicameral legislature and neither a presidency nor federal courts. But this made for a very weak central government, while the DSA wants an overweening Washington, D.C., shorn of the inherent checks on the popular will that come with a multi-layered federal system. In short, it hopes for what Lord Hailsham, in his criticism of the British parliamentary system, famously called an “elective dictatorship.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a speech last week in which he inveighed against left-wing extremists who seek to destroy rather than build, targeting “the physical embodied symbols of power and invention and achievement.” He might have added to the target list, with a nod to the DSA, the U.S. constitutional order; the socialists have met the enemy — and it is our own longstanding, highly successful governing institutions. 130 Park Place, Alpena, MI 49707 - Copyright © The Alpena News We won't sell or share your personal information to inform the ads you see. title: Stop press: UK Supreme Court decision in Tesla v InterDigital & Avanci (via Passle) - Bristows
content: The UK Supreme Court has today decided that the UK court has jurisdiction to determine claims challenging the FRAND rates offered by SEP holders as part of pool or platform joint licensing. In this case, Tesla had brought proactive proceedings to enforce the FRAND obligations of SEP holder InterDigital (a member of the Avanci 5G Platform) to seek a decision from the UK Court as to whether that Avanci 5G Platform licence rate is FRAND. The first instance court and Court of Appeal declined jurisdiction to determine Tesla's licensing claims, but the UK Supreme Court has now overturned the decision meaning that Telsa can now continue to pursue the claims before the English court. FRAND obligation on joint licensing: there is a serious issue to be tried that a SEP owner is subject to the FRAND obligation when choosing to offer a licence of their SEPs though a licensing pool or platform. FRAND licence to the whole platform: for an SEP owner that is a member of the platform, there is a serious issue to be tried as to whether the FRAND licence of their SEPs is a licence to the platform rather than a bilateral licence (i.e. Tesla has a real prospect of establishing that the only FRAND licence for InterDigital SEPs is a global licence to the Avanci 5G Platform). Declarations as to FRAND rate for the platform licence: Tesla has a real prospect of being granted the declarations it sought, including whether the Avanci 5G Platform rate is FRAND and, if not, what the FRAND rate is. Jurisdiction: the claims in question are properly characterised as concerning a FRAND licence in respect of InterDigital's UK SEPs, notwithstanding that Tesla argues that only a global platform-wide licence would be FRAND. As such, the UK court has jurisdiction over the claims. Appropriate forum: there is no more appropriate forum to determine the claims. In the parallel proceedings before the Delaware Court of Chancery, the court would not, on the balance of probabilities, determine a FRAND rate based on non-US patents. In a change in tide, this decision shows that the licence rates for SEPs licensed on a pool or platform basis are not necessarily insulated from scrutiny of the courts. Whilst a decision on the merits is to come, this is the first step in allowing claims of this type can be brought in the UK and to pave the way for a new dimension of FRAND litigation. 100 Victoria Embankment London EC4Y 0DH T +44 20 7400 8000 DX 269 Avenue des Arts 56  1000 Bruxelles  Belgium  T +32 2 808 7500 18-20 Merrion St Upper  Dublin 2 , D02 XH98  Ireland  T +353 1 270 7755 This site uses cookies. title: Canon EOS R6 V firmware v1.1.0 finally adds flash support - Camera Jabber
content:
Canon has released firmware version 1.1.0 for the EOS R6 V and the EOS R6 Mark III, and for R6 V owners it delivers the feature many have been waiting for since launch: flash support. When the R6 V was announced back in May, Canon confirmed that external flash support would follow in a firmware update rather than being available out of the box — and this is the company making good on that promise. Both updates are available now from the Canon UK support pages. For the EOS R6 V, the headline addition is support for external flash units, bringing with it flash firing, E-TTL balance, E-TTL II metering, slow synchro, flash function settings and flash custom function settings. Alongside that, the update adds support for Canon’s BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller — with functions assignable to Remote function buttons 1 and 2 through the Customize buttons for shooting menu — plus a grid display during movie recording and support for Canon’s Software Development Assistance Kit (EDSDK/CCAPI). Several bugs are squashed too, including an issue affecting shooting when auto power-off triggered during interval timer shooting, a problem with the camera not being recognised over USB when connected to a smartphone, and incorrect movie digital IS metadata at frame rates below 24fps in Slow & Fast Motion mode. It’s worth being realistic about what that flash support actually means in practice, because the R6 V’s hardware sets the limits. The camera has no mechanical shutter, which caps the flash sync speed at 1/60 sec — a significant constraint if you’re trying to overpower daylight outdoors. It also lacks the traditional five-pin hotshoe, so it works natively only with flashes designed for Canon’s Multi-function Shoe, with older units requiring a compatible adapter. This is a video-first camera, and the flash implementation reflects that: genuinely useful for indoor fill and controlled situations, but not a route to serious strobist work. The EOS R6 Mark III gets a similar, slightly lighter update. It also gains BR-E2 support, the movie-recording grid display and SDK support, and inherits a feature introduced on the R6 V: AF for close-up demos can now be set during movie recording in Movie manual exposure, Movie auto exposure and other Creative Zone modes, working in combination with exposure and AF area settings. That’s the setting which overrides face detection when you hold an object up to the camera — a boon for anyone shooting product demos or unboxings — and it was previously restricted to one specific mode. Neither update is transformative, but both are welcome. Canon following through on a stated launch commitment is worth acknowledging, and the close-up demo AF trickling across to the R6 Mark III is exactly the sort of quality-of-life improvement that makes a camera nicer to live with. Adds support for external flash units (flash firing, E-TTL balance, E-TTL II metering, slow synchro, flash function settings, flash C.Fn settings). Adds support for the BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller, with functions assignable to Remote function buttons 1 and 2 via Customize buttons for shooting. Adds grid display during movie recording. Adds support for the Software Development Assistance Kit (EDSDK/CCAPI). Fixes an issue affecting shooting ability when auto power-off activates during interval timer shooting; an issue where the camera may not be recognised when connected to a smartphone via USB; and incorrect movie digital IS metadata when recording below 24fps in Slow & Fast Motion Movie mode. Note: flash sync is limited to 1/60 sec as the camera has no mechanical shutter, and native compatibility is limited to Multi-function Shoe flashes. Adds support for the BR-E2 Wireless Remote Controller. Adds grid display during movie recording. Adds the ability to set AF for close-up demos during movie recording in Movie manual exposure, Movie auto exposure and other Creative Zone modes, for use in combination with exposure and AF area settings. Adds SDK support, along with bug fixes. Both firmware updates were announced on 22 July 2026 and are available to download now for Windows and macOS from Canon’s support site. title: Trump v. Slaughter: Future Hurdles For DPF-Based EU And UK Data Transfers To The US? - JD Supra
content:
Last month’s Supreme Court decision in Trump v. Slaughter has created uncertainty about the long-standing position of the independence of the Federal Trade Commission. This, in turn, has prompted Max Schrems and his NGO (NOYB) to renew concerns about the Data Privacy Framework (DPF). They have asked the European Commission to review its conclusion that transfers made to participants in the program were adequate under GDPR. It is based on this that the UK adopted its “data bridge” for UK-US transfers. The Court’s decision surrounded Trump’s removal of two FTC commissioners. One of them, Slaughter, challenged this decision; however, in its recent decision the court ruled the President could fire Commissioners "at will" and was not restricted to the historic position relating to their conduct in office. According to the Court, the FTC exercises executive power and therefore falls under the authority of the President, who can thus appoint and remove Commissioners without cause. Schrems argues that as a result of this decision, the FTC is not acting sufficiently independently, and as such cannot be a true independent enforcer of the DPF. And, he argues, it was that independence on which the EU based its adequacy decision. Additionally, he states that reliance on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) may similarly be flawed. Namely, because those rely on transfer impact assessments (TIAs) that assume independent oversight by the FTC. Putting It Into Practice: We do not anticipate that the EU will repeal its adequacy decision on its own. However, this recent statement from Schrems and NOYB suggests that the Framework may be in for a challenge. European or UK companies that transfer data to those in the US, and those who receive such data in the US, should anticipate this. Practical steps to prepare include (1) taking stock of data that is flowing, (2) the basis on which the transfers are being made, and (3) assessing if additional protection measures should be put in place. title: Jackler v. Merit Systems Protection Board - Constitutional Accountability Center
content:
In Jackler v. Merit Systems Protection Board, the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit is considering whether the Trump administration can ignore critical civil service laws when removing Immigration Judges. Until February 2025, Megan Jackler and Brandon Jaroch were Immigration Judges (IJs) charged with “conduct[ing] specified classes of proceedings” involving immigration law. They were abruptly terminated in violation of federal civil service law, which provides that IJs can only be removed for cause and with at least 30 days’ advance written notice. When Jackler and Jaroch invoked these protections before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the Trump administration advanced a novel claim—that because IJs are “officers of the United States,” Congress cannot impose any limitations on the Attorney General’s authority to remove them. The Board agreed, and the IJs appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which agreed to hear the case en banc. In July 2026, the Constitutional Accountability Center filed an amicus brief in support of the IJs. Our brief explains why the Trump administration’s argument is at odds with the text and history of the Constitution, as well as centuries of historical practice. First, the Board relied on the argument that IJs are inferior officers, but the executive does not possess limitless power of removal over those officers. The Constitution gives Congress great flexibility in determining how best to shape the federal government, as well as a unique authority over inferior officers. In the nation’s early years, legislators recognized that Congress’s authority to create inferior offices and provide for their appointment necessitated control over their removal. Even lawmakers who contended that the President should have an inherent power to remove high-level officials agreed that Congress had authority to regulate the removal of inferior officers—it was widely assumed that any presidential power of removal extended only to officers appointed by the President. Second, Congress has regulated the appointment and removal of inferior officers since the Founding. In the early republic, both Congress and the President seemed to understand that the president’s removal power was something to be granted—it had to be specified or it did not exist. As the nineteenth century progressed, Congress began explicitly regulating removals more frequently. And in the era after the Civil War, Congress tackled the “spoils system,” when public offices were corruptly doled out by political parties. It reformed the civil service to promote greater independence from party politics, and it began to protect inferior officers from arbitrary or politically-motivated removal. Finally, the Supreme Court has confirmed Congress’s power to govern the removal of inferior officers and employees. As early as 1886, the Court explained that Congress has the power to “limit and restrict the power of removal as it deem[ed] best for the public interest” in the case of inferior officers. For over a century afterwards, the Court repeatedly held that Congress controls removals in the case of inferior executive officers. While the Supreme Court recently overruled the precedent holding that Congress can create “expert agencies led by a group of principal officers removable by the President only for good cause,” it relied on historical evidence that specifically addresses the removal of high-level officers and explicitly declined to “determine the fate of officials not before [it].” Its decision provides no basis for extending that removal power to inferior officers supervised by the Attorney General. title: Supreme Court Eliminates Private Medicaid Provider Requirement Challenges - Legis1
content: The Supreme Court's decision in Medina v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic eliminates a crucial legal tool that Medicaid beneficiaries and providers have used to challenge state exclusions of health care providers from the program. The ruling reshapes the landscape for private enforcement of Medicaid requirements and opens the door for states to restrict which providers can serve low-income patients without fear of private litigation. The implications extend far beyond abortion policy, potentially weakening beneficiary protections across the entire Medicaid program. In June 2025, the Supreme Court issued a 6-3 decision authored by Justice Neil Gorsuch that fundamentally altered how Medicaid disputes reach federal court. The case centered on a straightforward question: whether individual Medicaid beneficiaries can sue states under federal law when a state violates Medicaid's any-qualified-provider requirement, which mandates that state Medicaid plans allow beneficiaries to obtain services from any qualified institution, agency, community pharmacy, or person capable of delivering the service. The Court held that Medicaid's any-qualified-provider requirement does not confer a privately enforceable right under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983, the Civil Rights Act provision enacted in 1871 that allows individuals to sue state actors for violating federal rights. This means beneficiaries can no longer file private lawsuits to challenge provider exclusions. Instead, enforcement now rests primarily with the HHS Secretary, a shift that significantly limits remedies available to affected patients. The decision emerged from South Carolina's 2018 executive order directing the state to terminate Medicaid enrollment for abortion clinics. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic and a Medicaid beneficiary sued under Section 1983 to block the exclusion. Both the district court and the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the plaintiffs, finding that the any-qualified-provider requirement created an enforceable right. The Supreme Court reversed. Justice Gorsuch's majority applied the Gonzaga University v. Doe standard, which requires that a law must clearly and unambiguously use rights-creating terms and display an unmistakable focus on individuals to support a Section 1983 claim. The Court used the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act provisions from Health & Hospital Corp. of Marion County v. Talevski as the yardstick for determining rights-creating language. The Medicaid statute, the majority concluded, fell short of that standard. The Court expressly rejected reliance on two earlier precedents: Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Association and Blessing v. Freestone. These cases had suggested broader pathways for enforcing Medicaid requirements through private litigation. In Wilder, the Court had found that health care providers seeking to challenge Virginia's Medicaid reimbursement rates had a right to sue. The Medina majority effectively reversed course. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored a dissent joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan. The dissenters argued that the any-qualified-provider provision easily satisfies the unambiguous-conferral test. They pointed to the original session law title "Free Choice by Individuals Eligible for Medical Assistance" as evidence of rights-creating language. The dissent warned that the majority's approach effectively turns the analysis into whether Congress imitated the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act, a standard the dissenters viewed as unworkably rigid. The decision arrives amid intense congressional conflict over abortion funding. Congress passed P.L. 119-21, the FY2025 reconciliation law, which included Section 71113, imposing a one-year funding restriction prohibiting Medicaid payments to certain providers that furnish elective abortion services. Planned Parenthood and more than 20 states filed suits challenging the constitutionality of this provision. A Massachusetts district court issued preliminary injunctions temporarily blocking enforcement against the plaintiffs, but the First Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction in the Planned Parenthood case. The one-year funding restriction expired on July 4. The Medina ruling has given states a new legal foundation to pursue provider restrictions. Some states have sought to continue excluding abortion providers from Medicaid participation and have cited Medina as a legal basis for doing so. This creates immediate political pressure on the administration to respond through enforcement mechanisms now concentrated in the HHS Secretary's office. The administration must decide whether and how aggressively to withhold federal Medicaid funds from states that exclude qualified providers, a blunt instrument compared to the private litigation pathway the Court has now closed. For Republicans, the decision represents a significant victory in the broader effort to limit abortion access and funding. For Democrats and abortion rights advocates, it removes a crucial legal remedy and shifts enforcement from courts to executive discretion, which changes with administrations. Medina v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic fundamentally shifts power away from individual beneficiaries and providers seeking to enforce Medicaid requirements. The ruling means that states can now exclude providers, whether for abortion services or other reasons, without facing private lawsuits from affected patients or providers. In South Carolina, over 1 million Medicaid beneficiaries are directly affected by the inability to access Planned Parenthood services following the state's 2018 exclusion policy. The decision weakens legal protections across a wide range of Medicaid law. According to the Kaiser Family Foundation, the Medina ruling opens the door for other states to exclude specific providers from Medicaid without facing private litigation, and it directly enables state-level efforts to exclude Planned Parenthood from Medicaid without fear of successful private lawsuits. The Georgetown University Law Review has noted that the decision weakens legal protections across a wide range of Medicaid law. Practically speaking, beneficiaries harmed by provider exclusions now have no direct recourse in federal court. Enforcement depends entirely on HHS action, which may or may not materialize depending on political priorities and administrative capacity. title: Honda CR-V vs Toyota RAV4: The Most Reliable SUVS You Can Buy Compared - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update If you are on the market looking for an SUV in 2026, it's very likely you will come across either the Honda CR-V or Toyota RAV4. Being two of the most popular Japanese SUVs on the US market, these models have every reason to be loved by customers throughout the years. Solid reputation, great market value, efficient powertrain options and an impeccable reliability record. In this article we are taking a close look at CR-V vs RAV4 reliability, to see which one of them is more dependable over the long run. This article examines the reliability of the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4 over the past three generations by comparing their common issues, recalls and customer complaints according to NHTSA and J.D. Power. Ever since the first-generation CR-V launched in 1997 with a utilitarian vibe that was loved by customers, this compact SUV has been one of the most successful Honda models to ever exist. Blending the outdoor vibe with daily usability, the CR-V has come a long way since the first generation. But regardless of which generation you go for, you will always get Japanese reliability along with the versatility that has made the CR-V a favorite among customers over the past two decades. The current CR-V is in its sixth generation, being introduced to the US market in 2023. It is available in pure gasoline form or as a hybrid. There is even a hydrogen-powered fuel cell model called the e:FCEV. Considering the variety of options available on the sixth-gen CR-V, it's not a surprise to see a 19.3% sales increase when compared to the previous year. This increase in sales also makes the CR-V the best-selling SUV in the US market for 2026 so far, dethroning the Toyota RAV4. "We're already wondering if the CR-V in hybrid form might be the best small family crossover on sale right now. Everything essential for the class, from the calibration of the suspension, steering, and drivetrain to the comfort and controls in the cabin, strikes us as just right for the segment." It wouldn't be a stretch to say that the Toyota RAV4 kickstarted a new segment by itself. When the first-generation XA10 was introduced to the US market in 1996, this Toyota SUV started a revolution in the automotive landscape that would turn the compact SUV segment into one of the most popular segments in the modern automotive landscape. While it has been two decades since the first RAV4 hit the US market, the rugged outdoor vibe is still evident even in the brand-new sixth-gen RAV4. Entering into 2026, the Toyota RAV4 is completely redesigned with a sharper exterior look and a more refined interior. The new sixth-gen RAV4 is available as both a conventional hybrid or a plug-in hybrid model. Other than the efficiency of the hybrid powertrain, the new RAV4 is also available with three distinctive exterior designs that suit various types of customer. Along with the rugged Woodland trim that's been available since the previous generation, the GR Sport model adds an aggressive look to the RAV4 for the first time. While it's not news that the CR-V is a reliable SUV with a solid reputation and robust powertrain, there are still a couple of common issues that you should be aware of before picking one up. The first common issue that can be found across multiple generations is battery drain and alternator failures. It's therefore important to replace old batteries and alternators and look out for signs such as weak cranking and dim dash lights. Other known issues that have been commonly found on CR-V models over the years are the failure of air conditioning. The symptoms include unusual noise when switching on air conditioning, loud noise and buzzing from the dashboard. It's worth noting that a replacement or a rebuild to the compressor can be costly most of the time. Only address the issue if symptoms are present. Owners have also reported a jerky shift and vibration during acceleration from the models equipped with a CVT transmission. This issue is particularly prevalent in the fourth and fifth generation CR-V, in which the models have received complaints that are related to the CVT transmission. The complaints include a delay in shifting and heavy vibration during idle and acceleration. Transmission issues can normally be fixed by a torque mount or software upgrade. Nothing is perfect. The same goes for the reliability of the Toyota RAV4. It may be one of the most reliable SUVs you can buy in 2026, but here are some common issues you should be aware of. The first is related specifically to the hybrid models, especially fourth- and fifth-generation models. The weak 12V battery would sometimes cause a complete system shutdown. We would recommend checking the battery regularly, especially in colder climates, and driving the vehicle routinely to charge up the battery. As for the transmission, sharing the same symptoms as the CR-V, certain RAV4 that are equipped with the CVT transmission are also reported by the owners to have hesitation under light throttle. This is especially evident during stop-and-go traffic. Make sure to keep the transmission software up to date and conduct service on a regular basis to prevent such issues. Considering the popularity of these two models, there is a high chance that you will look for one on the secondhand market. While they have remained mostly consistent in terms of reliability throughout the years, here are the years that we recommend staying away from. For the Honda CR-V, it's the 2015 model from the fourth generation, and 2017 and 2018 models from the fifth generation that pose the most issues. According to J.D. Power, all three model years have received an average rating for quality and reliability, with the 2017 model receiving the lowest score of just 76 out of 100. As for the recalls and complaints reported by NHTSA, the 2017 model is also the one with most recalls, receiving seven in total. While the 2018 model also has a total of five recalls and a whooping 2094 complaints. The issue that plagued the fifth generation Honda CR-V is mainly related to the engine, which could potentially lead to stalling and loss of power at speed. As for the fourth generation, which received 3 recalls and 668 complaints for the 2015 model year, the issues are mainly attributed to vibration issues with the engine and malfunction with the transmission. As for the Toyota RAV4, the 2019 and 2020 models from the fifth generation have proven problematic for owners throughout the years. Both the 2019 and 2020 models have received a score below 80 for the quality and reliability rating by J.D. Power. The lower score is mainly attributed to the eight-speed transmission, which owners have reported severe lurching, delayed engagement and hesitation at low-speed. To get the best possible reliability out of these Japanese compact SUVs, here are the model years that you should focus on when buying one from the secondhand market. While the early model years for the fifth-generation Honda CR-V have proven to be problematic, the latter years for the fifth-gen CR-V received a better rating from J.D. Power and fewer complaints to the NHTSA. The 2022 model year is the one with the best rating, receiving 82 out of 100 in the quality and reliability rating. A total of three recalls and 232 complaints are also significantly lower when compared to earlier fifth-gen models. If you have a higher budget, the newer sixth generation is also a solid choice, with all model years receiving a score above 80 for the quality and reliability rating by J.D. Power. As for the Toyota RAV4, it's pretty much the same story, with the latter revised models receiving a better reliability rating. While the first two model years of the fifth-gen RAV4 are plagued by transmission issues and lower ratings from J.D. Power, the latter 2022 model year has fixed those issues and received a solid 87 out of 100 reliability rating. The reports have also been reduced to just a single recall and 135 complaints over the years. For those who are looking for a fourth-generation RAV4, the 2018 model is also a superb choice. With a score of 88 from the quality and reliability rating by J.D. Power and just three recalls and 328 complaints, making it the highest ranked fourth-gen RAV4 you can buy on the market currently. So you may ask, how much are you actually paying for these compact SUVs if you wish to buy one in 2026? Depending on their year and condition, their price can vary quite a lot, but we are here to give you a rough idea of how much they might cost on the market in 2026. Starting with the Honda CR-V, the first model year of the fourth generation is 2012, which has an average market of $12,881. Some better examples could potentially go up to $20k, and you might also get ones which cost less than $10k if the conditions are less desirable. For the fifth-gen CR-V, which spans between 2017 and 2022, you are expected to pay somewhere between $18k to sub-$30k for this Honda SUV. For the latest sixth-gen CR-V, be prepared to pay somewhere around $30k, as the majority of them cost more than $30k. As for the Toyota RAV4, the fourth generation that was on the market between 2013 and 2018 has a price range roughly around $10k to $20k. Some early examples will have a price tag of sub $10k while newer models tend to cost somewhere close to $20k or even higher. The Supreme Court has decided that UK courts have jurisdiction to hear a claim for declarations as to whether the rates and terms offered for global pools of standard essential patents (SEPs) are fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND). By its claim, Tesla seeks a declaration that the rate of $32 per vehicle offered by the Avanci pool for a 5G global licence is not FRAND. In the High Court, Fancourt J held that it was “obviously of interest to implementers like Tesla to know whether the non-negotiable terms that are offered by Avanci are FRAND”, but that UK courts had no jurisdiction so to decide. In the Court of Appeal, the majority agreed with Fancourt J, but Arnold LJ gave a dissenting judgment explaining why he would have allowed Tesla’s appeal. The Supreme Court has unanimously allowed Tesla’s further appeal, holding that: (i) Tesla has a real prospect of successfully arguing that (a) the FRAND obligation applies to a pool licence offer (paras 79-92), (b) the only FRAND licence under InterDigital’s UK SEPs on the Avanci platform is a pool licence (paras 93-105), and (c) declaratory relief can fairly and properly be granted (paras 106-145). (ii) Tesla’s claim is properly characterised as relating principally to InterDigital’s UK SEPs on the Avanci platform (paras 154-177). (iii) Tesla’s claim was properly served on InterDigital under CPR 63.14 (paras 178-193) and passed through Gateway 3 as regards Avanci (paras 190-193); and would in any event have passed through Gateway 11 against all defendants (paras 194-203). (iv) The Delaware Court of Chancery was not an alternative available forum for the determination of the dispute (paras 204-216). James Segan KC acted for Tesla in the High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, instructed by Powell Gilbert LLP.

title: Canon EOS R6 V Review: A Pro Vlogging Camera At A Mirrorless Price - Engadget
content: With a 33MP sensor, RAW video, open gate and active cooling, it has few video limitations. Sony put the "V" in vlogging with cameras like the ZV-E1 and ZV-E10 II, carving out a creator niche that rivals failed to match for many years. However, Canon carefully bided its time; after releasing the R50 V last year, it recently unveiled the powerful 33-megapixel, full-frame EOS R6 V. It's a camera with pro video intent in a mirrorless body, with features like RAW and open gate video that Sony's rival ZV-E1 noticeably lacks. With the same sensor as Canon's mainstream R6 III and pro-oriented C50, the R6 V slots neatly between those two models, offering stabilization like the former plus the latter's active cooling. There are some compromises at the $2,500 price point, though, with the biggest one being the lack of an electronic viewfinder. I took the camera out in Paris and the French countryside and found it to be impressive for video, but not as great for photos. The first thing that struck me about the R6 V was a significantly chunkier body than I expected, largely due to the active cooling fan and dust- and water-resistant design. It's quite a bit thicker than the R6 III, though less slab-like than the C50. The magnesium and polycarbonate body is relatively light though at 688 grams, a touch less than the R6 III. The R6 V has a relatively generous complement of manual controls, including two dials on top, a joystick, a control wheel at back, a dedicated photo/video switch and a mode selector. Thanks to Canon's slick new button numbering scheme, a quick glance shows that it has exactly seven programmable buttons. By comparison, Sony's ZV-E1 is downright sparse with just a single control dial on top, a control wheel at back and no joystick. The extra controls make the R6 V a delight to use, allowing full manual operation with little need to dive into menus. The video and photo settings are firewalled from each other, so switching modes doesn't mess with your favorite settings. Canon's menu system is still old-school and a bit clunky compared to Sony's more modern menus, though, which makes finding some settings a chore if you're not used to Canon cameras. The R6 V has a rear three-inch display that flips out for multi-angle shooting and vlogging. The display's resolution is good at 1.62 million dots, but the screen is slightly lacking in brightness. As mentioned, though, it has no EVF, which makes shooting in sunlight difficult at times. To handle 7K RAW and C-RAW up to 2,600 Mbps, the camera comes with a single CFexpress Type B slot, along with an SDXC UHS II card slot for proxies and other less demanding formats. There are also microphone, headphone and full-sized HDMI ports, along with a USB Type C 3.2 Gen 2 connector for charging and file transfers. The R6 V is missing the timecode port found on the C50 and other pro cameras, however. The R6 V offers no-compromise video options, matching many pro cinema models feature for feature. You can shoot up to 7K 12-bit RAW video either in 3:2 open gate mode (6,960 x 4,640 at 30 fps) or 17:9 (6,960 x 3,672 at up to 60 fps) using RAW or RAW light codecs. 4K DCI RAW is also supported with a 1.5x crop, though I preferred shooting RAW at 7K to give myself cropping options and the sharpest possible video. If RAW footage takes too much card space, you can also use Canon's much lighter XF-HEVC S or XF-AVC S 10-bit formats in open gate 3:2 at up to 6,912 x 4,608, or 4K DCI at up to 120 fps with no cropping. If you do shoot RAW but also want a lighter option for editing, you can capture RAW on the CFexpress card and HD proxies on a UHS-II card simultaneously. With active cooling, overheating is mostly a non-issue with this camera unless you're filming when it's really hot outdoors. I tested the R6 V in demanding conditions, filming 7K light RAW at 60 fps at about 85 degrees Fahrenheit with the fan set to "high." Capture continued for 80-plus minutes with no issues until the battery died. Video autofocus is excellent, on par with the AF in Sony's new A7 V. In normal mode, the AF can quickly and accurately switch from one subject to another, thanks to the Dual Pixel AF II system. Subject tracking automatically detects people, animals and vehicles. Like the R6 III, you can register specific people if you want to prioritize them for autofocus. Another setting is "AF for close-up demos" that will quickly focus on a product put in front of the camera, much like Sony's "Product Showcase" feature. To test the subject AF, I found some ducks and other waterfowl at a park. The R6 V was swiftly able to detect and stay locked on the birds' eyes. When some ducks swam under a bridge, it instantly picked them up again when they emerged on the other side. It worked even better with people, locking tenaciously onto faces. I took closeup video portraits and it kept the eyes (not the eyelids or lashes) in sharp focus, even at a shallow f/1.4 aperture. Stabilization is also a strong point. The 7.5 stops of shake reduction is slightly less than the R6 III's 8.5 stops, but engaging the digital IS makes it highly effective for things like panning or even walking. There is one downside: The 33-megapixel sensor isn't stacked, so rolling shutter distortion can be an issue if you jolt the camera or pan too quickly. However, the sensor readout speeds are among the fastest for any non-stacked sensor, so I saw very few skewed and unusable shots. Video on the EOS R6 III was extremely sharp in the 7K RAW and the 4K HQ modes, though other 4K modes weren't quite as detailed due to pixel binning. When shooting people, wildlife and landscapes, Canon's color science was on point, delivering warm skin tones and accurate colors. In one tricky sunny day scenario, shooting birds on a pond and under a bridge, the RAW video allowed me to reduce bright areas and boost shadows with no noticeable loss in sharpness or color accuracy. Low-light shooting was also top notch, with noise under control up to ISO 6,400 and (provided exposure was correct) ISO 12,800. If you're a hybrid shooter that favors photography over video, I'd recommend the EOS R6 III or another camera like Nikon's Z6 III over the R6 V — mainly due to R6 V's lack of an EVF and mechanical shutter. That said, the R6 V isn't bad for photography in a pinch. Like the R6 III, the R6 V can shoot RAW bursts at up to 40 fps and allows pre-continuous shooting of 20 shots (0.5 seconds) before the shutter button is fully pressed. That was particularly handy when I was shooting birds that could move or fly unexpectedly. Autofocus for photography is also excellent. As with video, it includes automatic subject detection for people, animals and vehicles. It generally locked on to subjects quickly and reliably, even when I shot high-speed bursts of fast-moving subjects. However, Sony's A7 V AF is slightly better in photography mode, as I found it gave me fewer out-of-focus shots. Photos are sharp but dynamic range isn't on par with the R6 III. That's because the R6 V only has an electronic shutter that captures 12-bit RAW, not 14-bit RAW like the R6 III can in mechanical shutter mode. The result, I noticed, was more noise in shadow regions. In comparison, Sony's A7 V offers 14-bit RAW photos with both the electronic and mechanical shutter, and therefore delivers superior dynamic range. The 33MP sensor did deliver sharp photos, though, and the RAW mode allowed me to tease a lot of detail out of high-contrast shots with bright and shadowy areas. Low-light photos looked clean up to ISO 6,400, with skin tones more flattering than I saw with Sony and Nikon cameras. JPEG photos were sharp and true-to-life straight out of the camera as well, with nicely balanced sharpening and noise reduction. Some hybrid mirrorless cameras like Sony's A7 V are better at photography than video, but Canon's R6 V is squarely in the opposite camp. It's an outstanding vlogging and creator camera thanks to the stellar RAW video quality, excellent handling, in-body stabilization and reliable video autofocus. Photography isn't a strong point, though, and should only be used sparingly.. Competition is now fairly deep in this segment. Sony's aforementioned ZV-E1 is a decent full-frame creator camera, but its lack of RAW and open-gate video, along with the mediocre handling, puts it at a disadvantage to the R6 V. Panasonic's $3,200 S1 II offers RAW video, a partially-stacked sensor and creator-centric features but is significantly more expensive. Another solid option is Nikon's $2,200 ZR, which has the benefit of a partially-stacked sensor and RAW video, but the 24MP resolution limits video capture to 6K. If I were shopping for a vlogging camera in this price range, I'd be torn between Nikon's ZR and Canon R6 V. If higher 7K resolution and more reliable autofocus top your list of needs, choose the R6 V. However, if reduced rolling shutter and RED cinema camera compatibility are more important, the Nikon ZR is your best bet.

title: 2025 Honda CR-V Owner Drives a 2026 Toyota RAV4 450 Miles, Hits 44.5 MPG, But Still Refuses to Buy One Over a Key Interior Flaw - Torque News
content: That is real-world hybrid efficiency at its absolute peak. Yet, one long-term Honda owner is walking away from Toyota's crown jewel. When St. Louis resident Yvan Carr-Chua handed back the keys to a 2026 Toyota RAV4 loaner after logging 450 miles across Missouri interstates, rural highways, and surface streets, he was staring at a massive mathematical victory. His personal vehicle, a 2025 Honda CR-V Sport Hybrid, averages 33.8 MPG over 22,000 miles of daily driving, meaning the rival RAV4 handed him a staggering 10.7 MPG jump without a single change to his driving style. Despite that insane 600-mile range on a single 14-gallon tank, Carr-Chua is stubbornly refusing to jump ship to Toyota, exposing a major hidden rift in the compact SUV wars that window stickers completely fail to capture. As I have noted in my investigative analysis on Toyota RAV4 Hybrid vs. Honda CR-V Hybrid: There's Only One That Will Last 300,000 Miles, while Toyota’s planetary gear e-CVT architecture remains an absolute mechanical vault for ultra-high-mileage drivers, Honda’s cabin ergonomics present an entirely different level of daily refinement that legacy specs cannot measure. In a candid breakdown shared on the Honda CR-V 2023-2026 Facebook Discussion Club, Carr-Chua delivered an unvarnished owner-to-owner comparison that cuts straight to the root cause of why fuel economy alone no longer guarantees brand loyalty. “I’m currently in a 2026 RAV4 rental for the week and here’s my takeaway as a 2025 CR-V Sport Hybrid owner... Exterior: By far the best-looking RAV4 they’ve put out. Interior: Meh… same old song and dance from Toyota. If somewhat rugged, somewhat childproof, and lots of plastic is your vibe, then this is the vehicle for you. The lines feel dated, the cuts aren’t luxurious, and the materials are lackluster... Infotainment greatly outclasses the CR-V... Fuel Economy: If this is your top item, I’ve never seen anything like this... I’m getting 44.5 mpg with zero adjustment to my driving style at all! Holy crap. 600 miles to a 14-gallon tank is insane... In conclusion, I personally would not purchase one, as I’m loyal to Honda, and prefer the nicer interior design.” That single assessment highlights the exact tactical tradeoff drivers are silently making on dealership lots across North America today. A comprehensive multi-vehicle comparative report from U.S. News & World Report Automotive Division notes that "the cabin quality, with its high-end materials and user-friendly technology, gives the interior a finish that reflects Honda's consistent investment in the tactile quality of its most accessible models." Why does a buyer willingly forfeit nearly 11 extra miles per gallon just to stay inside a Honda? The root cause isn't found on a standard brochure; it resides deep within the structural assembly and material science of modern vehicle dashboards. Toyota deliberately engineers the RAV4’s interior around hard, high-durability polypropylene plastics to lower manufacturing overhead, meet strict fleet durability targets, and provide a "childproof" cabin that resists severe scratches over a decade of abuse. However, those rigid plastic panels lack the acoustic damping layers and micro-foam backings that Honda integrates into the sixth-generation CR-V’s honeycomb dash architecture and isolated structural subframes. When you drive over expansion joints at 70 mph, those hard plastic cutouts in the Toyota transmit high-frequency vibration directly into the cabin, creating what Carr-Chua described as a "clunky dash cluster placed along a flat, water slide of a plastic dashboard." As I revealed in another field investigation, Honda CR-V Hybrid Owner Rents 2026 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Rejects Its High Seating Position and Rough Ride Quality, Honda achieves its buttery acoustic advantage by utilizing a specialized, lightweight aluminum front subframe that is completely rubber-isolated from the primary unibody chassis. Industry-wide metric tracking from independent review groups like Ralph Honda Technical Analysis further confirms that while Toyota leans heavily into a rugged aesthetic, "the RAV4’s entry-level and mid-tier trims feature practical interior materials that do not match the sophisticated tactile experience and premium leather-wrapped touchpoints engineered into the CR-V.” Rocky Mountain Altitude Testing Exposes The Real-World MPG Gap Living and testing vehicles here in Parker, Colorado, I regularly push these hybrid crossovers through severe elevation swings, sub-zero morning cold starts, and steep mountain passes along the Front Range. High-altitude atmospheric changes expose a fascinating engineering split between these two automotive giants. Toyota’s 2.5-liter naturally aspirated Atkinson-cycle engine paired with its dual-electric motor setup relies on aggressive engine RPM flare under load, which allows the engine to generate massive efficiency sweet spots on flat Midwest terrain—explaining Carr-Chua’s insane 44.5 MPG run in Missouri. However, up here at 6,000+ feet above sea level, that same Toyota powertrain screams loudly under hard acceleration, vibrating through that hard plastic dashboard and disrupting the peace of the cabin. Honda’s two-motor direct-drive hybrid powertrain operates more like an electric vehicle, using its 2.0-liter gas engine primarily as an onboard generator, which keeps cabin decibel levels significantly lower during high-stress mountain climbs. While Colorado drivers might see their fuel economy drop closer to the 34 MPG mark due to thin air and steep gradients, the acoustic insulation of the CR-V creates a calm, luxury-adjacent environment that hard plastic utility vehicles simply cannot replicate. If Toyota clearly dominates the raw mileage test while Honda wins the cabin refinement battle, which hybrid setup actually survives long-term mechanical abuse without throwing catastrophic diagnostic trouble codes? The immediate answer boils down to your regional climate and long-term ownership goals. If you live in a snowy, road-salt state where high-voltage corrosion is a constant threat, Honda’s simplified direct-drive hybrid transmission eliminates the vulnerable rear high-voltage harness layout that has plagued older RAV4 models. Conversely, if you live in a dry climate, drive 30,000 miles annually, and view your crossover purely as a tool to haul kids and gear, Toyota's bulletproof planetary gear train will easily march to 300,000 miles long after the plastic interior trim has aged. Yvan Carr-Chua’s week-long test proves that vehicle purchasing decisions are no longer decided by a single impressive stat line on a window sticker. Toyota built an incredible fuel-sipping powertrain wrapped in a rugged appliance, but Honda built a cohesive, comfortable daily sanctuary that owners simply enjoy sitting in every single morning. title: Fury v Joshua closer but hurdles still to clear - BBC
content: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have not shared a ring since a sparring session in 2010 The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Britons Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua has moved a step closer after they won their respective warm-up fights - but not without plenty of drama. Fury was first into the ring on Friday, stopping 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in seven rounds in Thailand. Joshua's night in Saudi Arabia was a different story. Facing little-known Albanian Kristian Prenga, Joshua was expected to ease through his comeback. Instead, he was dropped after just 20 seconds and again in the opening round before producing a stunning turnaround to stop Prenga in the second. With both men winning and contracts already agreed, the biggest fight in British boxing remains on course. Reports have suggested purses of about $100m (£75m) each, so there is every incentive to get the deal over the line. After chaotic return, where does Joshua win leave Fury fight? Many expected Fury to fly straight from Thailand to Saudi Arabia for a face-off inside the ring after a Joshua win. Remarkably, the only time they have ever shared a ring was during a sparring session at Finchley Amateur Boxing Club in 2010. After beating Wach, Fury insisted he would not travel to Jeddah and, despite rumours throughout Saturday, he kept his word. Reporters even briefly thought he had arrived when a Fury lookalike stepped out of a car outside the arena. But Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn insisted a fight with Fury will happen next. "It's done. We signed a legally binding contract about three months ago," Matchroom's Hearn said. Netflix is expected to broadcast the fight globally to more than 325 million subscribers, but the biggest unanswered questions are when and where. New York's Madison Square Garden in November is understood to be among the leading options as Saudi organisers look to maximise the event's appeal in America. British fans, understandably, want the fight in the United Kingdom - specifically at Wembley Stadium. Saudi boxing chief Turki Alalshikh has previously suggested if the bout were staged in Britain, it would have to start in the early hours of the morning to cater for the lucrative American television audience. It would not be unprecedented. Ricky Hatton's fight against Kostya Tszyu in Manchester in 2005 began at about 02:00 BST while Joe Calzaghe's victories over Jeff Lacy and Mikkel Kessler also started after midnight. Cardiff's Principality Stadium would welcome the opportunity to host Fury-Joshua, but the fight would have to be held on either Saturday, 31 October or Saturday, 28 November. The three Saturdays in between all host Wales rugby internationals. Wembley Stadium's curfew is 23:00, although London Mayor Sadiq Khan and Brent Council have indicated they would be open to discussions about extending it for this major sporting event. However, sources close to the mayor told BBC Sport on Friday organisers had not been in touch. Joshua knocked down twice as dramatic win sets up Fury fight Fury wins low-key warm-up to keep Joshua fight on track Joshua and Fury have signed separate contracts with Alalshikh, who is financing the fight. Hearn, however, insists their agreement is for the bout to take place in Britain. "We insisted that this fight was in the UK," Hearn said. "I know that AJ will sometimes want to be a little bit of a peacekeeper but the reality is he said to me 'I want the fight in the UK. This is a British fight'. I can't agree more. "We would have conversations but the only way the fight doesn't take place in England is if Anthony Joshua and myself agree to it because we have a legally binding contract." Joshua also made his preference clear after his win. "I wouldn't expect it to be at Tottenham [Hotspur Stadium] or the [Cardiff] Principality Stadium, respectfully," he said. "It's just got that history when you think of Wembley." Hearn says if Saudi organisers decide they want to stage the fight in America instead, Joshua's contract would need to be renegotiated. Fury's manager Spencer Brown told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Tyson would prefer it to be at Wembley, but if it's not at Wembley, he's not going to pull out of the fight. "We all want it in England, we all want it for the British fans. It's an iconic fight. But we're not the promoters, we're not the people that put the money in. "If I had to put my money down, it would be a choice of two for me: Wembley and New York." From a purist's perspective, the fight comes years too late. Fans wanted Fury and Joshua to meet when both were world champions and at the peak of their powers rather than after years of negotiations, failed talks and defeats. Other super-fights have also arrived later than many hoped, including Floyd Mayweather's victory over Manny Pacquiao in 2015 and, closer to home, Amir Khan's defeat by Kell Brook in 2022. Commercially, though, Fury v Joshua remains enormous. Joshua's knockout of Jake Paul introduced him to a wider American audience beyond traditional boxing fans, while Fury has built a huge following through his appearances on WWE, trilogy with Deontay Wilder and his Netflix series. Fury and Joshua are two of Britain's biggest sporting personalities. For casual fans around the world, that is reason enough to tune in and to sell out any stadium or arena. Highlights: Joshua beats Prenga after being in trouble early Joshua's comeback against Prenga was one of the bravest performances of his career but it also highlighted familiar vulnerabilities. Dropped twice by a heavyweight competing at world level for the first time, he somehow recovered to produce a dramatic stoppage victory. Joshua was fighting for the first time since surviving the car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele. The emotional burden was obvious afterwards as he struggled to speak during his post-fight interview. His recent results and performances do raise eyebrows. Since the end of 2023, Joshua has beaten Otto Wallin, former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, YouTuber-turned-boxer Paul and the unknown Prenga. The last time he faced a top-level operation, he suffered a damaging knockout defeat by Daniel Dubois. Fury has not looked untouchable either. Before comfortably beating Wach, he outpointed Arslanbek Makhmudov in April but had previously lost back-to-back world title fights to Oleksandr Usyk. His split-decision win over Ngannou in 2023 also came after he was knocked down by the MMA star. Perhaps the question is no longer who is the better heavyweight, but who has declined the least. Joshua still possesses knockout power but Fury's movement, ring IQ and adaptability make him the favourite.
