title: The Most Aggressive-Looking Harley-Davidson V-Twin Cruiser - Top Speed
content: Few motorcycle brands carry as much visual weight as Harley-Davidson, and nowhere is that more apparent than in the cruiser segment. The Motor Company has built its identity on big, bold, chrome-laden machines — and the current lineup reflects that, with a total of 10 cruisers spanning seven Softails and three Sportsters. Most lean heavily on retro styling, staying well within the brand's established design language. But a handful push things further, trading classic elegance for something rawer and more confrontational. We dug through the entire lineup to find the most aggressive-looking of the bunch — here's what we found. Out of our three picks, it's the Breakout that takes the cake by a mile. Why, you ask? Because of its aggressive dragster-style chopper look. The 21-inch front wheel is a rare sight for cruisers in general, and the same can be said for the beefy 240-section rear. Add to that the uber-long wheelbase, and what you have is a certified head-turner. We also dig the available color options, including Centerline Yellow, Brilliant Red, and our favorite, Midnight Firestorm with flame graphics. In second place is the Low Rider S. It's always been an aggressive cruiser in the H-D lineup, thanks to its chopper-esque design and burly overall stature. There are some nice design touches here, such as a small headlight cowl, blacked-out mechanicals, a sporty front fender, and alloy wheels. But the closer you look, the more the Breakout edges ahead. For instance, the air filter assembly and fuel tank both have much less visual drama on the Low Rider. The Breakout's two-into-two exhaust is also our preference over the Low Rider S's single exhaust. Last but not least is the Sportster S. It's an entirely different design from the Softails, drawing inspiration from old-school flat track bikes. The balloon-type tires, minimalistic body panels, and a distinct headlight give it a unique identity that many new-age riders appreciate. The upswept exhaust is a genuinely cool design element, even if it's not the most practical choice when carrying a pillion. For us, though, the Low Rider S and Breakout both feel more true to the H-D formula. That said, design is deeply subjective — feel free to disagree with us in the comments. Let's dive deep into the design of the Breakout. Up top, it features a sleek LED headlight and nacelle — more minimalistic than the previous-generation model. A closer look also reveals LED turn signals and chrome triple-trees to hold the forks. In the middle, the air cleaner sports a larger, more integrated shape. The tank, tail, and saddle carry over from the prior generation. Despite its retro chopper roots, the Breakout is a thoroughly modern machine. Harley has equipped it with a full rider-aid suite comprising cornering traction control, cornering ABS, drag-torque slip control, and ride modes. Practical extras like TPMS, cruise control, a USB Type-C port, and updated switchgear round out the package. Our only gripe remains the basic semi-digital instrument cluster, which looks identical to Harley's more affordable Nightster. For a bike at this price point, we'd expect something more premium. All those electronics exist for good reason: there's a serious powerplant beneath the skin. The Breakout runs the Milwaukee-Eight 117 Custom engine, producing 104 horsepower and 126 pound-feet of torque — figures that represent meaningful gains over the previous iteration. All that power reaches the rear wheel through a six-speed transmission and belt drive. Turning to the underpinnings, the Breakout is built around a steel double-cradle chassis. Suspension duties are handled by Showa 49 mm dual-bending telescopic forks up front and a Showa monoshock at the rear — only the latter offers adjustment, via hydraulic preload. Braking comes courtesy of a single disc at each end, which feels modest given the bike's fully fueled weight of nearly 700 pounds. On the plus side, that massive 240-section rear tire remains one of the widest fitted to any production cruiser, and it pairs with the chopper-inspired 21-inch front wheel to striking visual effect. Harley has worked hard to make sure you don't feel all that mass on the move. The seat sits just 25.6 inches off the ground, the footpegs are forward-set, and the tubular handlebar is wide and relaxed. The two-piece saddle looks genuinely spacious, with a dedicated section for a pillion passenger. The trade-off for that low, stretched-out stance is limited cornering clearance — lean angle tops out at under 27 degrees in either direction. We want to hear from you. HMRC v BlueCrest Capital Management (UK) LLP [2026] This case review was co-authored by Charlie Middleton, Trainee Solicitor. On 1 July 2026, the Supreme Court gave judgment in HMRC v BlueCrest Capital Management (UK) LLP [2026] which concerned the salaried members rules in the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005. In this eagerly-awaited decision, the Supreme Court provided important guidance on when members of a limited liability partnership should be taxed as employees rather than partners. The decision will have significant implications for professional services firms, investment managers and many other businesses operating through the LLP structure. Following the introduction of LLPs in 2000, the structure has been seen by policy-makers as allowing LLP members, effectively operating as employees, to obtain the tax advantages associated with partnership status. In response, Parliament introduced the salaried members rules in the Finance Act 2014 to prevent so-called “disguised employees” and the LLPs from benefiting from self-employed tax treatment. Under the legislation, an LLP member will be treated as an employee for income tax and National Insurance purposes if each three of the following statutory conditions are satisfied: HMRC assessed that almost all of BlueCrest’s members satisfied each of the three conditions and therefore fell within the salaried members regime, the exceptions being members of BlueCrest’s original executive committee. It issued PAYE determinations of approximately £142 million, together with National Insurance liabilities of approximately £55 million. BlueCrest accepted that Condition C was satisfied but disputed HMRC’s conclusions in relation to Conditions A and B. The Tax Tribunal dismissed BlueCrest’s appeal on Condition A but allowed it on Condition B in respect of desk heads and portfolio managers with more than $100 million in capital allocations. That decision was upheld by the Upper Tribunal. The Court of Appeal set aside and remitted the Tax Tribunal’s decision on the basis that it had fallen into error on the application of Condition B. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected BlueCrest’s appeal on Condition A, agreeing with HMRC and each of the lower courts that the relevant remuneration arrangements constituted disguised salary. The majority of the Court’s decision focussed the interpretation of Condition B and, in particular, the meaning of “significant influence” over the affairs of an LLP. The Supreme Court held that the relevant influence must derive from the LLP’s legally enforceable constitutional arrangements. This includes powers conferred by the LLP agreement, statutory rights and authority validly delegated through the LLP’s governance structure. By contrast, influence arising solely from an individual’s reputation, commercial success, expertise or informal working relationship does not satisfy the statutory test. Importantly, the Supreme Court recognised that qualifying influence is not confined to powers expressly contained within the LLP agreement itself. It held that members exercising authority through management committees or other delegated governance bodies may possess sufficient influence, provided those powers ultimately derive from the LLP’s constitutional arrangements. This reflects the reality that many modern partnerships, including LLPS, delegate significant management responsibilities rather than concentrating them solely in the partnership agreement. The affairs of the LLP generally require a focus on managerial or strategic decision-making, although the Supreme Court left open the possibility that a member may have significant influence without having participated in such decisions in certain circumstances. The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Appeal that significant influence requires “a degree of influence… which has a practical and commercial substance in the conduct of those affairs in the real world”. Central to the judgment was the distinction between governance and performance. A portfolio manager may generate substantial profits and be commercially indispensable to the success of the business. They may exercise operational responsibilities. But that does not mean they exercise significant influence over the affairs of the LLP. The relevant question is whether they possess legally conferred powers enabling them to influence the management, direction or governance of the LLP itself. Commercial importance alone is insufficient. The Court considered that this interpretation best reflected Parliament’s intention. The legislation was designed to distinguish genuine partners, who participate in the management and governance of the business, from individuals who, despite being labelled members, are effectively employees in all but name. The Supreme Court has established that the Condition B enquiry focuses on legally conferred governance powers rather than commercial or operational influence.  In doing so, it seeks to provide more predictable, and accessible, framework for both HMRC and taxpayers when applying the legislation. The application of Condition B remains fact-sensitive. The Supreme Court noted that Bluecrest’s management structure was very “top-down” with significant authority being vested in the board and executive committee. However, those familiar with the operation of LLPs, particularly larger LLPs, will know that it is common for significant influence to be vested in particular committees or individuals. The Supreme Court’s confirmation of the narrower approach to Condition B should prompt LLPs and their advisers to review their governance structures and their approach to the salaried members rules generally. Firms should carefully consider whether members without significant influence would nonetheless be considered partners because either Conditions A or C exclude them from the salaried members rules. Where firms are reliant on members not meeting Condition B, they should consider whether members who genuinely participate in the management of the business have sufficient formal delegated authority to demonstrate significant influence, or whether existing governance arrangements require amendment. Conversely, LLPs should be cautious about assuming that senior operational responsibilities alone will be enough to satisfy Condition B. Firms cannot simply rely on the fact that an individual generates significant revenue or occupies a commercially important position. Instead, they should ensure that any governance powers exercised by senior members are properly reflected in the LLP agreement or other legally effective governance arrangements. title: Between stadiums, BTS' V turns to a book on quiet power of everyday life - The Korea Herald
content:
Between stadium performances and global commitments, BTS' V has drawn attention to a book that explores the quiet power of simply getting through everyday life. Late Thursday night, the singer shared on his Instagram story "The Sensibility of an Everyday Person" (a literal translation of the Korean title), a newly published essay collection by the celebrated Korean lyricist Kim Eana. The publisher, Storyseller, said messages poured in almost immediately after V shared the book. "Seeing the response the moment V shared the book reminded us just how much it means to authors and publishers when an artist introduces the books that have inspired them," the publisher wrote on social media. Kim reposted V's story on Instagram with a brief note of thanks addressed to the singer by his given name, Kim Tae-hyung. One of South Korea's most influential lyricists, V has written some of modern K-pop's defining songs, including Park Hyo-shin's poignant ballad "Breath," Brown Eyed Girls' era-defining dance hit "Abracadabra," IU's breakthrough anthem "Good Day" and Ive's self-affirming chart-topper "I Am." If self-help books often promise reinvention, Kim's latest collection argues for something more modest: returning to the rhythms of everyday life. Kim described the book as an exploration of "the small things that saved me when everyday life felt close enough to touch but somehow remained out of reach, when life seemed ever so slightly out of alignment and I felt alone in it." Kim turns her attention to those quietly sustaining an ordinary life. The essays offer comfort to readers who are simply trying to get through each day. "The days that unfold without dramatic highs or lows, without straying from their course, are proof that we're living earnestly," she writes. "How much time and effort does it take to simply keep that going?" Kim writes that finding happiness in such ordinary things is "a tremendous blessing." While everyone naturally strives for a better material life, the quality of that life ultimately depends on whether we have "small moments of happiness we can savor like pieces of candy along the way." The new collection is her first book in six years, following her 2020 bestseller "Ordinary Words," which has sold more than 200,000 copies. V's recommendation arrives as BTS enters another busy stretch. After wrapping up the European leg of its "Arirang" world tour, the group is set to begin performances across North and South America on Aug. 1. Iraola told reporters after the weekend win that Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Ryan Gravenberch have all arrived at Liverpool’s training base in Chicago (liverpoolfc.com), with the trio having enjoyed some time off after their involvement at the World Cup. All three know that they’ll be central to the head coach’s plans for the upcoming campaign, but this week is about each of them becoming acclimatised to how the Basque works in terms of training and in-game tactics. For Wirtz and Isak in particular, they’ll be determined to answer their critics from last season, with neither quite hitting the heights expected from them after their £100m+ transfers to Liverpool last summer. Although none of the returning trio solve the Reds’ glaring centre-back issues, Iraola will be quite glad to have them with the squad and begin working with three players who are likely to be fixed presences in his strongest starting XI for the coming season.

title: The Toyota Prius Makes The Honda HR-V Look Thirsty And Sluggish, And They Cost The Same - CarBuzz
content: Justin Pritchard is a seasoned Sudbury, Ontario-based automotive journalist, producer, and technical writer. With a passion for cars and a talent for storytelling, he's established himself as a prominent figure in the Canadian automotive scene. His work, which encompasses automotive reviews, insightful analyses, and stunning photography, is featured across multiple Canadian television programs, print publications, and online platforms. Justin's dedication to his craft has earned him numerous awards and accolades, solidifying his reputation as a trusted voice in the automotive industry. Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Most shoppers today buy SUVs, not cars, as a default solution for practicality and fuel efficiency. Could the Toyota Prius be the ultimate anti-crossover of the SUV scene? This slick, sleek hybrid hatch is a few hundred dollars worth of roof-mounted cargo carrier away from SUV storage capacity, and could cut your gas bill in half (or more) compared to something like a Honda HR-V. If you’ve stuck to your guns and avoided buying an SUV for years, the latest Prius is more worth a look today than ever, thanks to its latest-generation platform. As we'll see below, Toyota's famous hybrid challenges the compact SUV in numerous metrics, and makes many look thirsty, pricey, and sluggish in comparison. Examining this stacked pricing structure highlights how closely packed the entry-level options are compared to models at the top end. The base HR-V LX FWD has the lowest cost of entry on our list, but adding AWD or moving to the Sport FWD quickly closes the gap on the Prius. At just $28,755, the base Prius LE FWD slots directly between the mid-tier HR-V variants. Notice how the base Prius undercuts several mid-tier HR-V trims while including safety tech the HR-V charges extra for. But price parity only matters if the Prius can actually compete on what drivers experience behind the wheel. The Prius range also gives shoppers more high-end options to consider, with the HR-V line capped at $31,950 for a top-tier EX-L AWD, and the Prius range pushing beyond $37,000 for a Limited AWD. From a strategy standpoint, the HR-V sticks to an accessible $5,350 price span across all trims, but the Prius expands its reach across a broader $8,400 range, allowing for shoppers after higher-end tech and premium features. So the Prius matches the HR-V on price and beats it on standard features — but does it actually perform better, or does the hybrid system sacrifice driver engagement for fuel savings? The Prius doesn't just sip less fuel – it's genuinely faster than the HR-V, reaching 60 mph in under 7.5 seconds versus the Honda's nine-plus. Here's why the hybrid system makes that possible. With its hybrid system supplementing the gas engine, drivers get 194 horsepower in front-drive models and 196 hp with AWD. Note that the Prius’ AWD system uses an electric rear "e-axle", electrically driving the rear wheels without the need of a driveshaft for a physical connection to the front section of the powertrain. Numerous other Toyota models use this setup, as well. The HR-V instead uses a traditional AWD system and a traditional four-cylinder engine of 2-liter displacement, no hybrid gear added. That's good for 158 hp, giving the Prius an output advantage of 36 to 38 hp. While Toyota doesn’t provide a net torque output figure for it, the hybrid-electric torque from the Prius engine makes for low-rpm throttle response that’s sharper and more responsive than the HR-V’s, not to mention quieter. Between this pair, the Prius is the racier machine, not only in looks, but also in performance. Both the Prius and HR-V have fairly noisy engines, though the Prius manages some redemption by way of smoother and snappier performance to back it up. Both machines come in front- or all-wheel drive, both run a CVT transmission in all configurations, each runs just fine on 87-octane gas, and neither has a towing rating. According to EPA data, the Honda HR-V gets 28 combined MPG with front-wheel drive and 27 combined MPG with AWD, resulting in an annual fuel cost of $2,200 to $2,300. By comparison, the Toyota Prius delivers an impressive 57 combined MPG with front-wheel drive and 54 combined MPG with AWD, cutting annual fuel expenses down to around $1,125. The gas cost penalty of adding AWD to either machine is negligible, with the HR-V’s AWD system costing an extra $100 in fuel, and the Prius adding just $50 to your annual gas bill. In dollar terms, the Prius will cost about $1,125 per year less on fuel than the HR-V, despite its performance and output advantage. In this comparison, Toyota’s hybrid system gives drivers a 24-percent horsepower boost, while cutting fuel costs in half. If you keep either of these machines for five years, that amounts to nearly $6,000 saved on fuel costs alone. Beyond that, there is an additional penalty that the Prius allows HR-V shoppers to avoid. Driving the Honda HR-V in the city brings fuel efficiency down by as much as six miles per gallon, adding 20 percent to fuel consumption in city-cycle driving versus highway cruising. On the other hand, the Prius gets roughly the same fuel economy whether it's being driven in the city or on the highway, and the hybrid system actually makes front-drive Prius variants slightly more fuel efficient in the city (57 MPG) than on the highway (56 MPG). So, in addition to drinking about half the fuel of a Honda HR-V overall, the Prius' hybrid tech also shrinks the roughly 20-percent city-driving fuel consumption penalty to virtually nothing, or even reverses it slightly. Long-distance drivers should take note of the EPA-provided range figures as well: the Prius can go up to 644 miles with FWD, compared to the HR-V’s 392-mile figure. That’s an extra 252 miles per tank in the Prius, a64 percent advantage in driving distance versus the HR-V.On paper, the Prius dominates – but paper specs don't capture the one area where the HR-V fights back hard. Is a Prius a viable alternative to a slower, thirstier crossover SUV like the Honda HR-V? Maybe. When deciding between these two machines, it is important to bear a few additional factors in mind. Consider overall height. The HR-V sits about 7 to 8 inches taller than the Prius, a factor to consider if you’ll frequently be loading and unloading roof-mounted gear. If you’re on the vertically challenged side, the Prius’ roof-mounted accessories will prove easier to reach. Though the Prius cuts the fuel bill in half, it also has considerably less ground clearance than the HR-V. On the plus side, that helps with a sportier and more car-like ride that some drivers will like. On the downside, less ground clearance limits off-road capability, and can be an issue for drivers in climates that frequently see heavy snow and road slush. The HR-V has a suspension tuned for all-round comfort, and ride quality stands up well on rough road surfaces. Many drivers will find the Prius to feel sportier and more agile, though noisier and harsher when encountering poorly maintained asphalt. The HR-V offers the more spacious cabin overall, with 97.3 to 98.7 cubic feet of total passenger volume compared to the Prius’ 91.2 cu ft. That’s an advantage of at least seven percent for the HR-V, which also wins on headroom in both seating rows by no less than 0.4 inches and as much as 1.6 inches, depending on trim grade and seating position. Look for 1–4 percent more headroom for the HR-V driver, and more than 4 percent (1.6 inches) for rear-seat occupants versus the Prius. The Prius gives front occupants 1.3 inches (3 percent) more legroom, while the HR-V prioritizes rear passengers with significantly more rear legroom than the Prius, beating it by 2.9 inches (over 8 percent). Wide-shouldered occupants will have a better time in the HR-V as well, since it offers 1.3 inches more room up front and 2.4 inches more in the rear. Front hip room is virtually a dead heat, with the Prius holding a slight advantage, but pulling ahead significantly in rear hip room, where it beats the HR-V by 4.3 inches. On cargo hauling capability, the base Prius LE matches the HR-V almost cubic-foot for cubic-foot, offering 23.8 cu ft of space compared to the HR-V’s 24.4 cu ft. That’s a negligible difference of just 0.6 cu ft, roughly the volume of a medium-sized kitchen microwave oven. Stepping up to higher Prius trims (XLE, Nightshade, Limited) drops cargo capacity slightly to 20.3 cu ft due to interior packaging. Toyota doesn’t list a seats-folded cargo metric for the Prius, though we know the HR-V has the practical advantage of its shape when its rear seats are folded down, opening cargo volume up to 55.1 cu ft. Ultimately, the Prius might not be an outright compact SUV killer, but it’s a highly worthy alternative for the driver who doesn’t mind giving up a little roominess in exchange for some sleeker style, or installing that bike rack or cargo box when a little extra space is required. title: Sharon V. Frankenfield (Violette) - Star Tribune
content: Fridley - Age 89 of Fridley, passed away on July 9, 2026, at Regions Hospital after a brief illness with her loving family by her side. Sharon was born on June 24, 1937, and raised in Northeast Minneapolis and attended St. Anthony of Padua School Catholic High School. On January 27, 1957, she married Raymond Frankenfield and together they raised five rambunctious sons. They later divorced. Sharon was a Licensed Practical Nurse and, later in life, returned to Anoka-Ramsey CC where she obtained her Registered Nurse degree. She worked as a labor and delivery nurse at St. Andrew's Hospital, St. Barnabas Hospital, Metropolitan Medical Center, and finally at Hennepin County Medical Center. Her colleagues were an integral part of her life, and many of them became lifelong friends. The bravest among them allowed her to join their golf group which continues today. Sharon was independent, strong-willed, compassionate, and the loving center of her family; she was rarely at a loss for words—often giving encouragement or advice. Raising five boys was one of her greatest achievements, and she made every effort to be there for each one of them or their families whenever they needed her. Pictures of her family adorned her walls in all her residences throughout her life, and she paid tribute to the past and the present with numerous photos of her family and friends. Her sons often teased her about her culinary skills, but she loved to entertain, to show off her latest concoctions, and was always up for lunch or dinner at one of her favorite restaurants. The goodbye hugs were deep, heartfelt, and always followed by "I love you." Sharon's lifelong hobby was knitting, and her numerous mittens, hats, sweaters, shawls, blankets and kitchen rags can be found all over the United States. She could talk and knit at the same speed without even looking at her knitting needles. After her retirement, Sharon traveled extensively in the United States but also throughout Europe and the Pacific. Sharon's final residence for the past three years was at Hayden Grove Senior Living in St. Anthony where she was surrounded by many former residents of Northeast Minneapolis who shared her passions for cards, board games, emojis, and family. She was preceded in death by her parents George and Fern Violette; infant grandson Ross Allen Frankenfield; and brother-in-law Timothy Ready. Sharon is survived by sons Michael (Kelly), John (Beth), Greg (Marissa), Tom (Bonni) and Dave (Laura) Frankenfield; many grandchildren and great-grandchildren; brother George Jr. (Mary Kay) Violette; sisters Linda (Mike Sr.) Ojile; Mary Jo (Bruce) Durand; her ex-husband Raymond (Bev) Frankenfield; and a host of nieces, nephews, loving relatives and friends. A Celebration of Life service for Sharon will be held on August 29, 2026, at the Old Log Theater beginning with a visitation at 11:00 AM and a brief service offered by Father Henry Doyle at 12:30 PM. Food and fellowship will follow until 3:00 PM. Sharon's final wishes were that gifts or donations could be made in her name to Camp Knutson (campknutson.lssmn.org).    www.billmanhunt.com To send flowers to the family or plant a tree in memory of Sharon, please visit our floral store. title: V.com weekend vote: How much do you feel you can afford to pay for a set of strings? - Violinist.com
content: We have thousands of human-written stories, discussions, interviews and reviews from today through the past 20+ years. Find them here: July 25, 2026, 7:20 PM · This week the German-based string company Pirastro announced the release of a string set aimed at affordability, selecting some of its most popular strings for set that maximizes quality while offering a reasonable price point. Global inflation certainly has hit the world of violin, viola, cello and bass strings, affecting the prices of premium string lines in all brands, particularly in strings that contain precious metals such as silver and gold. (And in fact, some super-premium violin strings have spiked as high as nearly $500.) How does one cope? Many of us will simply shell out more to get the string brands we know, like and trust. Or we might change the strings a little less often. Or, we might look for quality at a lower price point. How are you feeling these days about the prices of violin strings, and particularly, what do you feel willing to pay for a set? Please participate in the vote below (which is in U.S. dollars, here is a converter if you need to figure this out for Euros, Canadian $, etc.). Then let us know your thoughts about the price of strings and how you are coping. July 26, 2026 at 12:45 AM · I've been fortunate in that the price of my current preferred viola strings (D'Addario Kaplan Amo) hasn't really changed since 2021. There have been a few temporary price increases due to supply chain interruptions, but the price has always dropped back down within two or three months. That said, inflation has made me more reluctant to try other strings. I've been meaning to try Peter Infeld, and I likely would have done it earlier this year if the price was still where it was 4-5 years ago. July 26, 2026 at 01:03 AM · As a pensioner, I tend to work out what things cost per month, and strings are a small part of my outgoings, so really the top price is more of a gut feeling. Luckily the Vision family suits my violin the best, so my upper limit is more or less fixed for me. I wonder if per month viola and cello strings cost the same as violin strings. July 26, 2026 at 05:16 AM · Many string sets now exceed $150 retail. July 26, 2026 at 11:57 AM · I don't change my strings but annually at most, so it's okay if they're more expensive.  I did find I like Warchal strings on my viola and my luthier can get them for $125. July 26, 2026 at 01:52 PM · I can get Visions for my viola for $100, so that works for me. July 26, 2026 at 02:51 PM · It's definitely gotten out of hand. If the higher-end strings lasted much longer than, say, Dominants, that'd be one thing, but I've found that pretty much any string set has noticeably declined after around 120 hrs of play, and at that point I'd rather just be playing a fresh set of Dominants I can get on sale for $58 rather than feeling guilty about having to stretch the lifespan of $140 Rondos to get my money's worth. July 26, 2026 at 03:36 PM · Yeah, I got Visions on my viola, Tom. But it's only a $500 viola, so there's no need to experiment further. It would be like putting lipstick on a pig. Lol. July 26, 2026 at 04:10 PM · My price limit would be whatever Pirastro gut Gold label is.  Finding the optimum set of strings is the least expensive way to improve the sound and response of a violin, but-- putting expensive strings on my inexpensive violins would be money half-wasted. July 26, 2026 at 04:33 PM · As a string program administrator, the cost of strings really adds up in our annual maintenance budget. Most of our teachers hate preludes so I had been working on finding a budget set that would be acceptable. Tonicas were already the right set. They sound similar enough to Dominants that teachers are happy and as the mom of a student in the program, I'm happy too. I tried Ascente and they were not acceptable to my ear. July 26, 2026 at 08:00 PM · Nickie, I can't say whether the wrapped E sounds better or worse, because that will depend on what sound and playing properties you like and dislike. A professional violist told me "I love the sound of your viola.  So, I will stick with them. The Merced County Association of Governments has released the 2026 edition of On the MoVe, its annual community report detailing how Measure V transportation sales tax dollars were spent across Merced County. The voter‑approved half‑cent sales tax generated $26.7 million in revenue during Fiscal Year 2024‑25 and invested nearly $15 million in transportation improvements countywide. The audited financial statements included in the report show, “total revenue: $26,762,905… total expenditure: $14,984,261.” Since Measure V took effect in 2017, the program has produced more than $200 million for road repairs, mobility upgrades and public transit. This year’s report highlights dozens of projects completed between July 2024 and June 2025, ranging from street rehabilitation and bridge replacements to sidewalk infill, bicycle infrastructure and intersection improvements. Every incorporated city in Merced County received Measure V funding, along with county‑maintained roads and regional corridors. Countywide, Measure V supported a wide range of transportation improvements. Examples highlighted in the report include the Lorraine Street Bridge replacement in Dos Palos, Palm Avenue rehabilitation in Merced County, and multiple sidewalk and street repairs in Merced, Livingston and Los Banos. The report also shows $2.3 million spent on alternative transportation modes, including bicycle and pedestrian improvements and investments in zero‑emission transit vehicles. Public transportation continues to play a major role in countywide mobility. Measure V’s free‑fare program provided 202,019 rides on The Bus’ fixed‑route system last fiscal year. Of those trips, 133,358 were taken by seniors, 63,366 by ADA‑eligible passengers and 5,295 by veterans. The report states that the program “helped residents access employment, medical care, shopping and other essential services.” MCAG Executive Director Stacie Guzman said the annual report demonstrates the value of the voter‑approved measure. “Every Measure V dollar spent represents an investment that Merced County residents made in their own communities,” Guzman said. The full 2026 On the MoVe report is available at mcagov.org/onthemove, with free printed copies in English and Spanish at all Merced County city halls and the county administration building.
